results.title: Craft Agents using Claude Agent SDK
results.content: # Craft Agents using Claude Agent SDK. ## Post details. ## Content. Hi everyone, Opus 4.5 and the new ways of SW development hit us as wrecking ball. Me and my CTO spent the last ~3-4 weeks to explore how AI-native SW development look like and how agentic flows can help day-to-day work. It is also open sourced under Apache 2.0 license. All feedback is welcome, but keep in mind it is a research preview, however we are also using it in our daily tasks. ## Top Comments. - Just installed it today, UI looks really good overall, I like the status idea to organise your chats. Couple of important points of feedback though (please let me know if you think it's user error): File search suggestions seems completely broken? When I start typing all my folders in my project show up, and some files do show up on rare occasions (I think when they're not too nested), but if i try to just type `@onboarding.tsx` or something it just doesn't show up. This hinders my workflow a lot. Even if i try to type the entire path, the file just does not show up. No ctrl+p and ctrl+n for navigating suggestions? This is pretty standard on Macos to move up and down suggestion popups. Kind of frustrating that you use yet another .{config} folder to add all my skills and stuff, I would have expected you to just pull from ~/.claude/ is this because you intend to add other AI providers and not just be a wrapper around Claude?? As above, more AI providers would be great, currently I'm planning to use Craft Agents for Claude work, and the new Codex app for GPT work. Would be even better if this just met all my needs and I could just use one app for everything + IDE for thorough reviews and manual coding when required. I understand the app is open source so I might submit some Issues and PRs when I have a bit more time. But great first impression overall, also Craft Docs is a great product too!

results.title: Inside a five-year-old startup’s rapid AI makeover
results.content:
Balint added the concept of “Sources” to the Craft Terminal: the ability to add other data sources – APIs, databases, MCP servers – on top of Craft Docs. The customer service team then started creating automations for common support tasks like sending discounts to emails on academic domains. The implementation of using APIs for sources is pretty clever: an API source acts like an MCP server to the agent, but Craft Agents hijacks the request and adds the credentials needed without the agent having access to those sensitive credentials.

However, the terminal interface was not beloved by Craft’s users. On December 18, he shared the Craft Terminal Agent with 15-20 external beta users. Feedback was positive and they liked it, but there were complaints about the terminal environment: [...] The Craft team is in phase one: everyone is using the most capable models and finding out how the models boost their work. There will be time later to think about how to change workflows. Part of changing workflows comes pretty naturally by making changes to Craft Agents.

### Devs’ struggles

Several engineers are struggling with the sudden change and there have been resignations, as a result. One engineer quit shortly after Balint’s AI mandate, who was one of Craft’s early engineers and one of the very few devs who knew the codebase inside out. [...] > “Zendesk wanted to charge us $20,000 per year for an AI integration that – to me – did not feel powerful at all. Frankly, this was one reason I started to build Craft Terminal, and then Craft Agents: I figured we can do a lot better than this.
>
> All our customer support flows now run through Craft Agents. We only use Zendesk as a backend.
>
> I want us to move to an API-first customer support solution. It feels to me that Zendesk is a really complex UI, one that is really slow, has bad API hooks, and just keeps breaking our flow.
>

Most complaint emails fail not because the grievance isn't valid, but because they're poorly structured, emotionally charged, or unclear about what resolution is needed. ## The Jenova Solution: AI-Powered Complaint Email Writing. ### How the Email Writer Agent Transforms Complaint Writing. Jenova's **Personal Secretary** tracks response timelines and automatically drafts escalation emails when complaints go unanswered. The **Legal & Contract Advisor** can identify regulatory escalation paths—CFPB for financial issues, FTC for consumer protection, state attorneys general for local matters—and help structure complaints that meet agency requirements. The Email Writer handles routine complaints instantly, while the Legal & Contract Advisor provides guidance for complex or high-stakes situations. With consumer complaints surging across every industry and companies increasingly relying on AI to triage grievances, your complaint needs to be clear, professional, and structured for action. It learns your voice, structures your grievance for maximum impact, and generates complaint emails that are clear, professional, and calibrated for your specific situation.

results.title: How to handle customer complaints when the product isn't actually broken - Bellsystem24 Vietnam
results.content:
The most common mistake agents make with emotionally charged calls is going straight into account verification: order number, model name, purchase date. That sequence is procedurally correct but poorly timed.

When a customer is frustrated, they’re not in a state where rattling off order details feels natural. Getting hit with verification questions right away signals that the agent is processing a case, not talking to a person.

The better move is to spend the first 30 to 60 seconds just listening and reflecting back.

> “I hear you. You did the research, picked something based on what you read, and it’s not doing what you expected. That’s a frustrating spot to be in, and I’m sorry you’re dealing with it.” [...] Expectation gap complaints are harder for a few reasons:

 The product isn’t defective, so warranty coverage doesn’t apply and the agent can’t lean on that script
 The expectation came from a third-party source the company had no hand in writing
 The customer is emotionally invested because they did their research and still feel let down
 By the time they call, they may have already vented on social media or left a review

Handling these calls well requires a different kind of competency. Not just process knowledge, but genuine communication skill and emotional awareness from the agent.

## How to handle customer complaints in a call center

### Step 1: Acknowledge the frustration before asking for anything [...] This isn’t an admission that the product failed. It’s an acknowledgment of the customer’s experience, which is a meaningful distinction and one worth building explicitly into agent training.

### Step 2: Find out exactly where the expectation came from

Once the customer has settled, the agent needs to understand two things: what specifically they expected, and where that expectation originated. The goal isn’t to challenge them on it but to correctly identify the actual problem before trying to solve anything.

A useful open-ended question:

> “Can you tell me more about which feature wasn’t performing the way you expected? I want to make sure I’m understanding exactly what you’re seeing.”

results.content: Post that, and you reach a professional audience that can directly advance your career. But you have to say something you might regret. I've watched plenty of execs freeze at that edge. The second camp wins, and it isn't close. When I launched Agent Craft, my sixth company, I told the real version: I built around an assumption that didn't survive first contact with prospects, realised the value wasn't in an individual product but in a team one, then pivoted, rebranded from Influence Craft, and relaunched. That's not a "thrilled to announce" post. That's the human experience of working through a hard problem, which is exactly what LinkedIn is missing. If you've posted the hard version, the one with the sharp edges left on, I want to know whether it paid off or bit you. [...] Almost nobody using AI right now is doing it correctly, and it has nothing to do with the tools. Your AI problem isn't really about AI. It's about the data you never collected. The tools don't fall short. There's just nothing solid to feed them. I watch CEOs ask the same question over and over. What should I do with AI today? How do I integrate it? Where are the cost efficiencies, the profitability efficiencies? All reasonable. All the wrong question. For most small businesses to really use AI, the question is different. What can I do today to prepare me to use AI profitably in the future? Here's why that matters. AI is not human intelligence. It looks at patterns and data, finds the anomalies, and predicts. The current LLMs and transformer-based models everyone's excited about need data [...] it paid off. What I keep coming back to is that you don't need to be a scientist to get value from this. Product people are building features now, and a tool like this lets you check your instincts against history and data before you ship. That's the part I want to keep testing. -- Repost it to your network and follow for more. James Goddard, Co-founder & VP of Engineering Powered by Agent Craft
